Every short in the book was squeezed out, and the record went green anyway. QQQ fell 4.9% on the week and VIX rose 31% to 19.99, but the move inside the index was a megacap unwind with money rotating into value — so the beaten-down names this report was short all rallied hard. LOW +6.4%, CMCSA +5.9%, CPRT +5.2%, NKE +5.0%, AZN +4.5%. All five stopped out. Three of them stopped in profit because the trail had already climbed past the fill: NKE +1.60R, LOW +1.30R, CPRT +1.03R. The two that had not yet earned a free stop cost −0.82R and −0.17R. Mark-to-market slipped from 3.59R to 3.55R, but realised R rose from 1.18R to 2.00R — and for the first time in this series, closed R is positive. The book is now two longs, both green.

Account equity — the same record in money

R is a risk multiple: 1R = $500, a fixed 1% of the starting account, and it stays fixed whether the account is up or down. The curve below is the same record converted to money — real share counts, real fills, real exits, marked to the close every session. The two views agree to $3 across 18 positions; the gap is share rounding, because a position sized int($500 / risk) almost never risks exactly $500.

The shape is the part worth looking at. The account made money steadily for a month, peaked at $54,230 on 2026-10-02, then gave back $2,807 into the 10-08 squeeze — 5.18% from the peak, or 5.61% of the account. It has recovered about half of that since. Both squeezes cost real money and the record still ends up ahead, which is the only test that matters.

Does adding to a winner help? — the rule tested, not asserted

Correction — I had this backwards. An earlier build of this report said adding to MCD would have turned a +1.48R winner into a +0.23R scratch. That number came from a bug, not from the market: the add was being evaluated before the stop check on the same bar, so an add made late in the 09-23 session retro-actively raised a stop that price had already taken out earlier that morning. With the bar processed in the correct order, adding is better, not worse.

The argmax moved this week, which is the strongest argument against chasing it. A week ago the best setting over twelve positions was a +0.00R gate. Re-swept over fourteen, the top is now a plateau: +0.25R and +0.50R tie at +8.47R, with +0.00R 0.22R behind. The rule has been moved to the conservative end of that plateau, +0.25R, and the reason is concrete rather than statistical: the add a +0.00R gate allowed and a +0.25R gate refused was AAPL on 09-21 at +0.23R — a position that went on to stop out. Requiring a trade to be meaningfully in profit before adding is not a curve fit; it is the difference between adding to something that is working and adding to something that merely has not failed yet.
And it breaches the risk cap. Simulated forward, the adopted rule carries $3,245 of open heat — 6.5% — and with this week's two new shorts that is 8.5%, through the 10% ceiling and well through the 8.5% event-week ceiling. NKE reaches 412 shares three sessions before it reports. The extra R is not free; it is bought with size, and the caps below are what stop that size arriving all at once.

What has actually been learned

The trail is now carrying the record. Sixteen positions are closed for a banked 2.00R. Of the five stopped this week, three were taken out above their fill. That is the whole design: the stop is not there to be avoided, it is there to end the trade at a price the position has already earned. Nothing about this week was a good tape for the book — every single short went against it — and the week still added 0.82R of banked profit.

Two squeezes in nine sessions, two different outcomes, same rule. On 10-08 five positions stopped and mark-to-market fell 4.88R. On 10-13 to 10-16 five more stopped and mark-to-market fell 0.04R, because by then the survivors had ratcheted stops into profit. The difference is not skill or timing: it is how long each position had been allowed to run before the squeeze found it.

The long book is still the weak half, but it has stopped bleeding. Seven longs have produced -1.31R against 4.86R from eleven shorts. Every closed long is a loser. The only two longs that have ever worked are the two open right now — ABBV at +0.56R and XOM at +0.99R — and both were taken the week breadth first crossed back above 40%. That is a single observation, not a result.

The add study is frozen, and the reason is worth stating. The last full replay put adds at -1.07R across the record, measured to 10-09. It cannot be restated: the pre-10-02 cohort archive was destroyed in the container reset and a no-add counterfactual needs every original plan file. What is known is that the three positions carrying two adds each — CPRT, LOW and NKE — all closed green this week, at +1.03R, +1.30R and +1.60R. No add has been taken since 10-06, and none qualifies this week.

Eighteen positions, sixteen closed, 2.00R banked, 3.55R total. The green rate is 39% — this is a system that loses small often and wins large occasionally, and the only thing that makes that arithmetic work is refusing to widen a stop. Five of eighteen positions have reached T1; none has reached T2.

The logic, stated as rules

Every filter below is computed from split-adjusted daily OHLCV — nothing is discretionary, and nothing was chosen after seeing which names would pass. The rule set fuses four published frameworks: Weinstein's stage analysis for the regime a stock is in, Minervini's trend template for whether it is in a genuine Stage 2 advance, the Donchian / Turtle channel breakout for the trigger, and volatility contraction plus volume signature for whether the base is being accumulated or merely drifting.

Long — Stage 2 trend template (all seven must be true)

  1. Moving-average stack. Close > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, and close above all three.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA higher than 21 sessions ago and 50 SMA higher than 10 sessions ago — the trend is being renewed, not decaying.
  3. Proximity to high. Within 25% of the 52-week high. Leadership does not hide in the bottom of its range.
  4. Distance from low. At least 25% above the 52-week low — filters out dead-cat bounces off a Stage 4 base.
  5. Relative strength. RS in the top 30% of the universe, where RS is the IBD-style weighted excess return over SPY: 40% × 3-month, 20% each × 6-, 9- and 12-month.
  6. Liquidity. 20-day average dollar volume ≥ $50M, so a 10–40 share-lot or a spread fills without slippage.
  7. Base structure. Range depth ≤ 18% measured over the shortest of the last 25, 40 or 60 sessions that qualifies.

Long — setup trigger (base rules plus these)

  • Proximity to pivot. Price within 7% of the base high — close enough that a buy stop is a trade, not a hope.
  • Not extended. No more than 14% above the 50 SMA. A stock already 3–5 ATR extended is a bad breakout buy regardless of how good the trend looks.
  • Volatility contraction or accumulation. Either ATR% today ≤ its level 20 sessions ago, or ATR% ≤ 0.85× its level 40 sessions ago (the VCP signature); or up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≥ 0.95.

Short — Stage 4 breakdown (all six must be true)

  1. Inverted stack. Close below both the 50 SMA and 200 SMA, and 50 SMA below 200 SMA.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA or 50 SMA declining — supply is in control on at least one timeframe.
  3. Proximity to low. No more than 25% above the 52-week low.
  4. Damage done. At least 18% below the 52-week high — this is a broken stock, not a pullback in an uptrend.
  5. Relative weakness. RS in the bottom 30% of the universe.
  6. Distribution. Up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≤ 1.05 — rallies are not being bought.

Trigger adds: price within 7% above the 25/40/60-session base low, and not more than 14% below the 50 SMA (an already-collapsed stock mean-reverts violently and is a poor short entry).

Entry, stop and target construction

  • Entry. Stop order at the structural pivot — the higher of the base high and the 20-day Donchian high for longs, the lower of the base low and the 20-day Donchian low for shorts — plus a 0.10 ATR buffer through the level. No anticipation, no limit orders inside the base.
  • Stop. The wider of the nearest structural level (10-day extreme, base extreme, or nearest clustered S/R zone) offset by 0.30 ATR, capped at 2.2 ATR from entry. The Turtle system's 2N stop, with structure allowed to tighten it but never to widen it past 2.2N.
  • Target 1. Entry ± 1.5R. Take a third to a half off; move the stop to breakeven.
  • Target 2. The measured move — base height projected from the pivot — or 2.8R, whichever is further.
  • Trail. Once a position is on it is managed by this report every week, and the stop ratchets one way only. Each week the managed stop is the tightest of: the stop already in force; the 5-day Donchian extreme in the opposite direction offset by 0.25 ATR (horizon-matched to a 3–15 day swing, where the Turtle 20-day exit is far too loose); the price that caps remaining give-back at 1R; and the original fill once the trade is +1.0R or better. It is then floored 0.75 ATR away from the last close so it never sits inside the noise band. A re-issued stop can tighten risk on a live trade but can never widen it.
  • Sizing. Shares = $500 ÷ (entry − stop), capped at 30% of account notional per position.
  • Book heat. Total risk across every position — open, added-to and new — is capped at 15% of the account, cut to 13.5% in any week where a live position reports earnings inside the holding window. Heat is spent in a fixed order: positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.

How open positions are tracked

  • One position per symbol and side. The first plan to trigger opens the position. Every later week's plan for the same symbol and side is a management update — a revised stop and revised targets on the trade already on — not a second trade. Grading each week's plan file as an independent cohort double-counts every carried position, and that is exactly what the earlier scorecards in this series did.
  • Selection is a union, never a filter. The weekly book is this week's screen picks plus every still-open position. The sector cap, the breadth rule and the setup-ready filter govern new entries only. None of them may drop a live position out of the book, because the result is a real position running with a stale stop that nobody is watching. The build fails if any open position lacks a card.
  • Re-entry is allowed, repetition is not. Once a position closes the symbol goes flat, and only a plan issued after the close date may open a new one — so the book never re-enters on the same stale level twice.
  • T1 takes half off, it does not close the position. Half comes off at Target 1 and books 0.75R; the balance rides the same daily trail toward Target 2 with its stop moved to at least breakeven. Booking the whole position at T1 caps every winner at exactly 1.5R while every loser is free to run to −1R, and the trail is what is supposed to pay for the losers.
  • Adding to a position that is working. A position is added to when this week's plan re-issues the same side at a trigger beyond the fill and the position is already through the gate. Half a unit per add, at most two per position. After an add the stop on the whole position moves so combined open risk stays at 1R of the original unit — an add can never turn a winner into more than a 1R loser. Never add back after Target 1 has been taken: scaling out and buying back in are two decisions that cancel, with two lots of slippage.
  • What blocks an add. Four separate guards, any one of which is enough: the name reports earnings inside the holding window; breadth is below 40% and the add is on the long side, because adding shares to a long is owning more long exposure and the no-new-longs rule covers it; the name no longer passes its side of the screen; or the add does not fit under the book heat cap. Heat is spent in a fixed order — positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.
  • Why adds rank ahead of new entries. Adding to a position that is already working is a higher-probability use of the same risk than a fresh trigger that may never fill — roughly a third of planned triggers never do.

How the levels on each chart were derived

  • Swing highs / lows. Fractal pivots — a bar whose high is the strict maximum (or low the strict minimum) of the five bars either side of it. Marked ▼ and ▲ on the charts.
  • Support / resistance zones. Three-bar fractal pivots from the last 15 months, clustered where they fall within 0.6 ATR of each other. Each zone carries a touch count and the date it was last tested — a level touched four times is a different object from one touched once.
  • Volume profile. Six months of daily bars, 80 price bins, each bar's volume distributed uniformly across its high–low range. POC is the highest-volume bin; the value area is the 70% of volume around it; HVN are local maxima above the 75th percentile (shaded purple — price tends to stall and rotate there); LVN are local minima below the 25th percentile (grey dotted — price tends to move through them quickly).
  • Donchian channels. 20-day and 55-day extremes, excluding the current bar.

Sources

Minervini trend template criteria — Deepvue, TraderLion on stage analysis. Donchian breakout lengths, the N/ATR volatility unit, 2N stop and 20-day trailing exit — the original Turtle trading rules. Volume-profile HVN/LVN/POC methodology — AlgoVistra, FXOpen on fixed-range volume profile. Price data via Yahoo Finance; live quotes, option chains, Greeks and the earnings calendar via the connected brokerage MCP.

Market regime

The index fell and breadth rose. SPY lost 2.0% to 763.25 and closed below its 50-day (768.50) for the first time in this series; QQQ lost 4.9% and sits 7.0% off its high; VIX jumped 35% to 19.99, touching 22.31 intraday. Yet the share of the universe above its own 50-day rose again, from 42.3% to 45.8% — the highest reading of the series. Stage 2 advances rose to 14.3% and Stage 4 breakdowns fell to 15.5%; for the first time, Stage 2 and Stage 4 are within 1.2 points of each other. An index falling while the average stock improves is not a decline. It is a rotation out of the names that carry the index.

This is a megacap and AI unwind, not a market decline — and the book is positioned on both sides of it. The long screen has expanded to 24 passers and 19 setup-ready names, the most of the series, and the accumulation readings are the best ever recorded here: XOM 2.42, AAPL 2.10, V 2.10, ABBV 1.95, PFE 1.91. They are staples, energy, health care, payments — value. The short screen is the mirror image: APP 93.4, ORCL 89.5, AVGO 86.7, TTD 83.4, TSLA 81.2. All five are the same trade. So the book takes four longs and one short, and the one short is the single highest-scoring name rather than five correlated versions of it. The squeeze that cost 4.88R two weeks ago happened because ten shorts were one position; that mistake is not repeated on the other side.

What the leadership is telling you

Value leadership, on volume rather than price. KO leads the long screen at 85.0 with up/down volume 1.62 and sits 0.2% off its 52-week high. AAPL (84.3, 2.10), XOM (83.9, 2.42), KDP (82.5, 1.79), LLY (81.5, 1.77), ADP (81.4, 1.18), CVX (81.4, 1.48) and PFE (81.3, 1.91) follow — eight names scoring above 81, every one of them within 3% of its high, every one of them on a 25-day base. A month ago this screen had eighteen passers and the best up/down reading was 1.75. It now has twenty-four and five names above 1.75.

The short side has narrowed to one theme. AppLovin at 93.4 is the highest short score this report has produced. Behind it: Oracle 89.5, Broadcom 86.7, The Trade Desk 83.4, Tesla 81.2. Up/down volume runs 0.33 to 0.87 — genuine distribution. But they are a single factor bet, and a bounce in AI would take all five out on the same morning.

What this means for the next report. If breadth holds above 45% while SPY stays below its 50-day, the rotation is real and the long screen is the place to be. If breadth rolls back under 40% with VIX above 22, the rotation was the first leg of a broad decline and every long on this page is wrong.

Why some high scorers were not given plans

Three filters sit on top of the ranking. Sector concentration — the two-per-sector cap counts open positions. Extension — names more than 14% below their 50-day are refused because that is where squeezes start, and the last two weeks proved it twice. Setup-ready only — thirteen of the twenty-six short passers fail a trigger condition.

This week a fourth filter did most of the work, and it is not in the ranking at all: earnings dates. Every single candidate on the long screen reports inside the 3–15 day holding window, because it is the second half of October. The filter cannot discriminate when it excludes everything, so the response was to use the spacing of the dates instead. LLY was dropped — it scores 81.5 and would have been the fifth long, but it reports 10-30, the same morning as ABBV, and both are health care. CVX was dropped for the same reason against XOM: 10-30, same sector, same session. The four names that remain print on 10-27, 10-30, 11-02 and 11-04 — four different days.

Long plans — breakout / trend continuation

Four long cards — two live positions and two new entries. Breadth closed at a series-high 45.8% even as SPY fell below its 50-day, which is a rotation out of the megacaps rather than a decline. XOM and ABBV are open from 10-12 and are management-only: the actionable number on those cards is the revised stop, not the re-issued trigger. KO and AAPL are the two highest-scoring names in the universe and are new entries at full size. All 24 long passers and their charts are in the Scan results tab.

KO and AAPL — the book is net long for the first time
The lightest book of the series, and the first long-tilted one. Open heat is 2.0% — two positions, both green — after the squeeze closed everything else. Three new entries take it to 4.9% against a 13.5% event-week cap, leaving $4,291 unused. Four longs against one short, the first time this report has been net long. Nothing needs cutting and no add qualifies.

Read this before placing anything

Two positions are live, both long, both green. XOM at +0.99R with its stop twelve cents under the fill, and ABBV at +0.56R with its stop still 0.44R below the fill. Neither is free yet; XOM is one session from it.

Three new entries: KO and AAPL long, APP short. KO and AAPL are the top two names on the long screen; APP is the top name on the short screen by the widest margin in the series.

No adds. Both open positions are blocked by the same thing — earnings on 10-30, inside the holding window. XOM at +0.99R would otherwise clear the +0.25R gate comfortably.

The cap is 13.5%, not 15%. Every live position reports inside the window, which triggers the event-week reduction. At 4.9% used it is not binding this week; it is stated so the number in the budget panel is not a surprise.

Capital deployed is $51,715 — 103% of the account. That is a separate number from book heat and it is new to this report. Heat ($2,459) is what you lose if every stop is hit; deployed capital is how much stock you are holding, and there is no portfolio-level cap on it — only 30% per position. So the book as written needs a margin account, which the APP short requires in any case. Reg-T on $50,000 gives $100,000 of buying power, so it fits, but it is leverage and you should know you are using it.

On every open card the price labelled fill is what you are in at. The number that changes is the stop, and the worksheet on each card is how to move it between reports.

If you want adds to actually fire, the binding constraint is the event-week heat cap, not the add rule. That cap exists because two live positions report inside the holding window; it lifts on its own once those prints are behind us.

This week's decisions, in order

  • 1. Move the open stops to the "stop for Monday" figure: XOM 170.89, ABBV 272.48. Both are ratchets — if what you have working is tighter, keep yours.
  • 2. Place the two new longs. KO 94.24 buy stop, AAPL 348.82 buy stop. KO’s trigger is only 0.36% above Friday’s close, so it fills early in the week or it does not fill at all.
  • 3. Place the one short. APP 259.16 sell stop, 2.62% below Friday’s close. It needs follow-through to trigger, which is deliberate — a short into a 70%-IV name after a 64% decline should have to prove itself.
  • 4. Do not add to XOM or ABBV. Both report 10-30. The gate is met on XOM and the add is still refused; that is the earnings rule doing its job.
  • 5. One short, not five. ORCL, AVGO, TTD and TSLA all pass and all score above 81. They are the same trade as APP. Taking one is the position-sizing decision of the week.
  • ⚠ All five names report inside the holding window — KO 10-27, ABBV 10-30, XOM 10-30, AAPL 11-02, APP 11-04. ABBV and XOM print on the same morning, and both are live positions. Decide now whether you are flat, hedged or through those prints; do not discover the date on 10-29.
  • The book is net long for the first time. Four longs against one short reverses a six-week tilt. The record says the short side is where the money has been made ({'{:+.2f}'.format(4.86)}R against −1.31R), so this is the screen overriding the record, not confirming it.

Execution notes

  • Monday 2026-10-19 is the next session — a normal week. If a stock gaps through its trigger by more than 0.5 ATR, stand aside.
  • Both option structures expire 2026-12-18, 63 DTE — longer than the usual 35–55 band, deliberately. Every name in this book reports inside the window, and the November monthlies price that event risk straight into the premium. December sits past all five prints.
  • KO has the better structure. The 95/100 call vertical is 18% IV with 8,689 contracts open on the long leg; six spreads cost $945 and risk $446 at the underlying stop.
  • AAPL sizes to one contract. The 350/375 vertical is $25 wide, so a single spread already risks $388 at the stop. A second would breach the $500 per-trade limit. The share alternative is 33 shares.
  • APP is shares only. The Dec 260 put quotes 22.70 / 30.00 — a 28% spread at 70% implied volatility. Crossing both legs costs roughly a third of the structure before the thesis is tested. Seventeen shares, or nothing.
  • The stop ratchet is one-way. If a revised stop looks wider than what you already have working, keep yours.
  • Re-run the scan on any 2%+ index day. With VIX at 20 and SPY under its 50-day, that is now a live possibility rather than a formality.

What would invalidate this whole report

The standing invalidation was touched this week. It has read, unchanged for six weeks: VIX above 22 with SPY below its 50-day. On 10-16 VIX printed 22.31 intraday and SPY closed at 763.25, -0.68% below its 50-day of 768.50. Both conditions were met inside the session. VIX closed at 19.99 — under the line — so the rule did not fire on the close, which is what it is written against. But it was a touch, not a near miss, and the correct response to a touched invalidation is a smaller book, which is what this is: three new entries instead of ten, 4.9% heat instead of 13%.

What would make the long thesis wrong. Breadth back below 40% while SPY stays under its 50-day. That combination says the rotation was the first leg of a broad decline and the value names are simply late to it. Breadth has risen three weeks running — 31.4%, 42.3%, 45.8% — so a single week back under 40% would be a genuine break in trend, not noise.

What would make the short wrong. APP is 63.9% off its high with a 5.4% daily range. One positive AI headline takes it, ORCL, AVGO, TTD and TSLA up together. That is exactly why there is one of them and not five, and why the stop is 28.78 points wide for only 17 shares.

The earnings cluster is the real risk this week. Five positions, five prints, all inside the window, two of them on the same morning. No stop protects against a gap through it.
